title.en: Ground Maize Becomes Flesh: The People of Corn

region.zh: 危地馬拉高地庫馬爾卡赫（烏塔特蘭）（象徵性定位）

texts.period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 3, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

texts.license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: After the twins rise as sun and moon, the daykeepers grind white and yellow maize nine times, wash it, and the water becomes human flesh and blood. From this dough the first four men are made, who walk, speak, and see — people of corn, in truth.
summary.zh: 雙子昇日與月之後，日守者九次研磨黃白玉米，洗淨之，其水化為人的血肉。由此麵糰造出最初四人，能行走、言語、觀看——真實的玉米之人。

sensitivity.note: Living K'iche' tradition; the Popol Wuj is treated by some Maya communities as sacred counsel. Only published translations are paraphrased.

passages.text: Then the Framer and the Shaper speak with Heart of Sky about what the people should be made of, since the materials of the first attempts have failed. And Xmucane grinds the maize: nine grindings, of yellow maize and white, and this is the food that becomes the flesh of man.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: She washes the flour, and the water in which it is washed becomes the fat of the body, red and rising. So the four men are made of the ground maize, and their flesh is of the grain that the earth gives; they are shaped and given faces, and they are neither too soft like mud nor hollow like wood.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: Their names are Jaguar Quitze, Jaguar Night, Not-Right-Now Jaguar, and Moon Jaguar, and they walk without stumbling, speak without stammering, and do their work without being told. This, the text says, is what people are made of: ground corn, warmed by water — the food of the earth become the bodies that eat it.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Christenson 2003); not verbatim.

narrative.en:
The making of the maize people answers the question left open by every earlier creation: what material can hold a soul, a memory, and a prayer? Mud dissolved, wood lacked heart and mind, so the Framer and the Shaper ask what should be used, and the answer is the staple of the Maya world itself: maize. The Popol Wuj specifies the process in kitchen terms — the grandmother Xmucane grinds white and yellow maize nine times, washes the flour, and the wash-water becomes the strength and fat of human bodies. From this dough the first four men are formed, and their names mark them as Jaguars: Jaguar Quitze (Balam-Quitze), Jaguar Night (Balam-Acab), Not-Right-Now Jaguar (Mahucutah), and Moon Jaguar (Iqui-Balam) — ancestors of the K'iche' lineages.

These men are everything the wooden people were not. They walk without stumbling, they speak the names of their makers, they give thanks in words, and they see to the very ends of the earth — so far that they must later be dimmed, because a people who see everything rival the gods. The maize men are the first humans whose flesh is also their food: the same grain that feeds a household is, in this account, the substance of the household's bodies. This is the theological ground of Maya agriculture, of the corn-cycle festivals, and of the modern Maya saying that people are made of corn.

The episode belongs to the cross-tradition cluster of humans molded from clay (or from a primary substance): it parallels Ymir's flesh in Norse myth, Pangu's body in China, Purusha's limbs in India, and the clay figures of Sumerian Enki or Chinese Nüwa — but with a distinctive agricultural theology. In Mesopotamia and Greece the material is a problem of craftsmanship; in the Popol Wuj it is a problem of nourishment, of reciprocity between the field and the table. The ninth grinding and the wash-water carry the weight of ritual detail: these are kitchen acts, the daily work of Maya women, elevated to cosmogony.

Culturally, the maize-people episode functions as the founding myth of the K'iche' lineage system: the four named ancestors will divide into the lineages that hold political power at Q'umarkaj, and every later K'iche' council traces itself back to one of the four. It also grounds the taboo-like reverence for maize: wasting corn is a defilement of the bodies of the dead and of the living, since flesh is made of it.

functions: Founding myth of the K'iche' lineages (the four ancestors named in the text)
Theological ground of maize agriculture and corn rituals
Explains human nature as edible earth: flesh of the grain that feeds it

variants.name: Norse Ymir / Chinese Pangu (primordial being dismembered)
variants.text_tradition: Gylfaginning (Sturluson c. 1220); Chinese cosmogony of Pangu
variants.summary: In those cosmogonies the human body is the raw material of the world itself; in the Popol Wuj the direction is reversed — the world's grain becomes human bodies.

variants.name: Sumerian Enki & Ninhursag clay people / Hebrew Adam
variants.summary: The failed-or-successful molding of humans from clay parallels the mud and maize attempts in the Popol Wuj.

variants.name: Tzotzil / Chol corn-people versions
variants.summary: Colonial and modern Maya groups retell the corn creation with local god names and household detail.

title.en: Too Much Sight: The Haze Over the First Men's Eyes
title.zh: 過盛之視：初民眼前的迷霧

region.zh: 危地馬拉高地庫馬爾卡赫（烏塔特蘭）（象徵性定位）

texts.period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 3, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

texts.license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: The first maize men see everything — the ends of the earth and the arch of heaven — and give thanks for their birth. But their perfect vision rivals the gods, so a haze is breathed over their eyes like breath on a mirror: they see only what is near, and the fate of humankind is fixed as partial sight.
summary.zh: 第一批玉米之人能看見一切——大地的盡頭與天穹——並為其誕生致謝。然而全知之視足以匹敵諸神，遂如呼氣於鏡面般，一層迷霧吹上其眼：此後他們只見眼前之物，人類的命運就此定為部分的視界。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: The four men made of maize lift their faces and see everything: they look to the four quarters and the four corners, and they see the arch of the sky and the face of the earth to its ends. There is nothing they cannot see, and they do not need to walk to know what is far away, for their sight returns everything to them.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: Heart of Sky speaks about it: it is not right that they should see everything; their nature must be lowered a little. And a breath falls over their eyes like a mist over a mirror, and their faces are dimmed, and they see only what is close and clear; what is far no longer comes to them.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: So the first four men are like people, and they lose the great sight and keep the small one, and that is how it has been for their children. The remainder of their seeing is left to the daykeepers, who read what others cannot.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Christenson 2003); not verbatim.

title.en: The Wives of the First Men

region.zh: 危地馬拉高地庫馬爾卡赫（烏塔特蘭）（象徵性定位）

texts.period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 3, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

texts.license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: The first four men sleep without wives and call out for companions, and the gods bring them wives: Water Woven Water, Poultry Raised, Water Child, and Water Woven. With them the lineages multiply, and the household — not the council — becomes the unit of the living.
summary.zh: 最初四人無妻而眠，呼求伴侶，諸神遂為其帶來妻子：織水者、豢禽者、水之子與織水者。自此族系繁衍，家戶而非議會成為生者之單位。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: The first four men are made and see, but they sleep alone, and in their sleep they say: we have no wives; who will bear our children? And they speak this in the night, and the gods hear it and confer.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the Framer and the Shaper make women for them: Water Woven Water for Jaguar Quitze; Poultry Raised for Jaguar Night; Water Child for Not-Right-Now Jaguar; and Water Woven for Moon Jaguar. These are the wives of the first men, and they are beautiful in their weaving and their waters.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: With the women come children, and the children of the four houses multiply into the lineages of the K'iche': from Jaguar Quitze the great line, from Jaguar Night and Not-Right-Now the others, and Moon Jaguar alone has no line. Thus marriage, not the council, makes the people that the council will later govern.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Christenson 2003); not verbatim.

title.en: Tohil, the God Who Walks Unseen

region.zh: 危地馬拉高地庫馬爾卡赫（烏塔特蘭）（象徵性定位）

texts.period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 3, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

texts.license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: The first men call to their god Tohil, but he walks among them unseen, speaking only from a bundle. Each of the four houses receives its own hidden patron — Tohil, Auilix, Hacavitz, and the Jaguar — and the men's eyes fail whenever they try to look at them.
summary.zh: 初民呼求其神托希爾，但他隱形行走於其間，僅自神包中發聲。四家各得一位隱形守護神——托希爾、阿維利希、哈卡維茲與美洲豹——人們欲一睹其形，眼睛卻皆失效。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: The men of maize pray for their god and receive Tohil, but he is not to be seen: he comes to them wrapped in a bundle, and his voice comes from inside it. The four houses receive their patrons — Tohil for the first, Auilix for the second, Hacavitz for the third, and for the fourth the Jaguar of the night — and no one may look on them directly.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the men try to see the god, their eyes fail; they see only the bundle and the ground. So they speak to their gods by ear, and the gods answer out of the bundle, walking with them unseen on the roads of the beginning, saying nothing of their faces.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Christenson 2003); not verbatim.

title.en: Fire from Tohil: The Rain Extinguishes and the God Relights
title.zh: 托希爾之火：雨滅火而神再燃

region.zh: 危地馬拉高地庫馬爾卡赫（烏塔特蘭）（象徵性定位）

texts.period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 3, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

texts.license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: When rain falls on the first people, their fire is quenched and they shiver in the cold. Tohil produces fire for them by turning his sandal, and the other gods do the same; but the flame comes at a price, and the people warm themselves in the dark, burning the straw and grateful for the hearth they did not make.
summary.zh: 大雨落在初民身上，熄滅其火，他們在寒冷中發抖。托希爾轉動其涼鞋而產火，諸神亦然；然火焰有價，人們在黑暗中取暖，焚燒草稈，感激這非其所造的火塘。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Then a great rain falls on the first people, and their fire goes out, and the cold settles on them. They shiver and huddle, and say: we are cold, we have no fire. And they remember the god who walks with them unseen, and call on Tohil in the dark and wet.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: Tohil answers by turning his sandal, and fire springs from it; Auilix and Hacavitz do the same for their houses, and the fire comes into the cold of the beginning. The people burn straw and brush and warm themselves, and the fire is kept and fed and never allowed to die again.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: But Tohil sets the price before the flame: what is given must be returned, and the hearts of beasts and of men will come to him in payment. The people agree, being cold, and the covenant of fire is made in the dark, and the hearth becomes the altar.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Christenson 2003); not verbatim.

region.zh: 危地馬拉高地庫馬爾卡赫（烏塔特蘭）（象徵性定位）

texts.period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 3, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

texts.license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: Tohil names his price: the blood and hearts of beasts first, then of men. The first men give the hearts of birds and deer before dawn, before the sun can see; and when they cannot keep the covenant with beasts alone, they take the hearts of captives — the origin of sacrifice among the K'iche'.
summary.zh: 托希爾定其代價：先取獸血獸心，後取人心。初民於日出之前、日目未見之時，奉上鳥與鹿之心；當僅憑野獸無以履約時，便取俘虜之心——基切獻祭之俗由此而起。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Tohil speaks out of his bundle: 'Let me be honored, for your fire is mine. Give me your blood; give me the hearts of the beasts of the field.' And the first men agree and go out in the dark before dawn, before the sun can see them, and take the hearts of deer and birds and offer them to the fire they did not make.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: The god is pleased, but the covenant grows: Tohil says that his food is not deer alone, and that the hearts of men will also come to him. The first men ask which men, and the answer is: the hearts of those who are captured in war, not of your own houses. And so war and sacrifice are bound together in one word of the god.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: This is the beginning of the taking of hearts among the K'iche', and the reason the daykeepers rise before dawn: the offering is made where the sun cannot look, because Tohil's covenant is older than the sun and must not be witnessed by the light it made possible.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Christenson 2003); not verbatim.

narrative.en:
The Tohil covenant is the mythic constitution of K'iche' sacrifice and, by extension, of K'iche' political power. After Tohil supplies fire to the cold first people, he names his price in a single sentence of blood: give me your blood, the hearts of beasts first, and then, if the covenant is to be kept at full weight, the hearts of captives taken in war — never of the donor's own house. The first men agree, and the offering is performed under a curious rule: it is made before dawn, 'where the sun cannot see', because the covenant predates and funds the sun itself.

The scene does two things at once. First, it converts the practical dependence on fire into a permanent ritual economy: every hearth implies a debt, and the debt is paid in hearts. Second, it fuses war and worship: the Popol Wuj makes captive sacrifice not a cultic accident but a clause of the founding contract, which explains why later K'iche' kings present themselves both as warriors and as daykeepers, and why the ballgame courts double as places of execution. The Popol Wuj is candid that this is a covenant, not an orgy of cruelty: hearts of beasts suffice for most days; human hearts are the escalation of a contract whose terms the ancestors accepted knowingly, in the cold, before the sun rose.

In comparative terms the episode belongs to the cluster of 'theft of fire / civilizing gift' (Prometheus, Maui, Coyote) but with the polarity reversed: the fire is not stolen from the gods by a hero on humanity's behalf; it is granted by a god and invoiced to humanity, with the account kept forever after in the day count and the blood count. The Maya heart-offering that scandalized Spanish chroniclers is here given its own legal origin — not Aztec imitation (the K'iche' and Mexica rites are independent developments of a shared Maya lowland tradition) but a contractual theology in which warmth, light, and time itself are held on credit from Tohil.

For the calendar, the 'before dawn' rule matters: it ties sacrifice to the watch-keeping of daykeepers and makes dawn the boundary of two economies — the old one of Tohil and the new one of the risen sun. The Popol Wuj repeatedly returns to this border: what belongs to Tohil is done in the dark; what belongs to the twins' sun is done in the light.

functions: Founding charter of K'iche' sacrifice as covenant rather than caprice
Binds war captive-taking to ritual obligation, defining royal warrior-daykeeper roles
Explains pre-dawn timing of offerings: Tohil's covenant predates the sun

variants.name: Yucatec Chilam Balam sacrificial idiom
variants.summary: Yucatec texts record comparable 'payment of the katun' language for blood offerings, framing sacrifice as calendar-debt rather than divine whim.

title.en: From Tulan: The Departure of the Nations

region.en: Tulan (mythic place of origin), symbolic pin on the Gulf coast of Tabasco, Mexico
region.zh: 圖蘭（神話起源地），以墨西哥塔巴斯科州灣岸為象徵定位

texts.period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 3, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

texts.license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: At Tulan, the place of seven caves and seven canyons, the ancestors of the K'iche', Cakchiquel, Tz'utujil, and other nations receive their gods and their day-count, and the languages of the nations are assigned. Then they set out, and Tulan is left behind — the origin remembered as a departure, not an arrival.
summary.zh: 在七洞七谷之地图蘭，基切、卡克奇克爾、祖圖希爾等族之祖先接受其神與日數，諸族語言亦在此分配。隨後啟程，圖蘭被留在身後——起源被記憶為一次離去，而非一次抵達。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: There is a place called Tulan, of seven caves and seven canyons, where the nations were divided and their gods were given to them. There the ancestors received the count of days and the staffs of office, and there the speech of the K'iche' was separated from the speech of the Cakchiquel and of the Tz'utujil, each people assigned its own words.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: The fathers of the K'iche' — Jaguar Quitze, Jaguar Night, Not-Right-Now Jaguar, and Moon Jaguar — take their bundles: the god inside the wrappings, the staffs, the count of days. And they set out from Tulan with the other nations, each going its own way, and the going itself becomes the memory of the origin.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: It is said of the road that they wept on leaving: the place of their beginning was behind them, and nothing of it went with them except the bundles, the language, and the days. Whoever counts the days counts Tulan still.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Christenson 2003); not verbatim.

title.en: Crossing the Waters with the Staffs

region.en: Tulan (mythic place of origin), symbolic pin on the Gulf coast of Tabasco, Mexico
region.zh: 圖蘭（神話起源地），以墨西哥塔巴斯科州灣岸為象徵定位

texts.period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 3, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

texts.license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: The ancestors leave Tulan and cross the sea, walking on the sand bars with their staffs and bundles; the waters part and close behind them. Some say they crossed on the sea itself, made of mud; all agree that the crossing was the proving of the bundles and the arrival of the K'iche' in their own land.
summary.zh: 祖先們離開圖蘭，執杖與神包踏上沙洲渡海；水在其後分合。有言其踏浪而渡、行於泥上；皆同其渡越乃神包之考驗，亦即基切抵達其地之始。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: They cross the sea, the ancestors of the K'iche', walking on the sand that shows itself under the water, each with his staff and his bundle of the god. The water is on both sides, and the crossing is narrow; behind them the sea closes, and Tulan is beyond reach.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: In some tellings they cross on a bridge of mud that hardens under their feet; in others the sea itself opens as it did for no one else. What is certain in all of them is the order of the march: the bundles first, then the staffs, then the people, and the count of days kept aloud on the road.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 3 (Brasseur 1861; Christenson 2003); not verbatim.

region.zh: 危地馬拉基切省庫馬爾卡赫（烏塔特蘭）

texts.period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03 (city founded c. 1400s)

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 4, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

texts.license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: After wars and wanderings, the K'iche' lords settle on the spur of rock called Q'umarkaj — rotten cane — and build the council houses of the three great lineages. There the count of days, the god bundles, and the tribute of the subject towns are gathered, and the K'iche' kingdom takes the form it still had at the coming of the Spanish.
summary.zh: 歷經戰事與遷徙後，基切諸主定都於名為庫馬爾卡赫（腐竹）的石崗，建三大族系之議事之屋。日數、神包與屬邑之貢遂聚於此，基切王國成形，直至西班牙人到來。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: The lords come to the spur of rock that is called Rotten Cane, Q'umarkaj, and there they settle, because the rock is high and the canyons around it are deep. They build the houses of the three lineages side by side: the house of Jaguar Quitze, the house of Jaguar Night, and the house of Not-Right-Now, each with its council bench and its bundle of the god.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 4 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: There they keep the count of days and the tribute of the towns that have submitted, and there the mother of the lineage keeps the fire. The rock becomes the city of the K'iche' kingdom, and from it the lords go out to war and return to the benches to decide what has been taken.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 4 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: This is the city that the Spanish will burn: its benches are remembered in the Popol Wuj as the place where the lineage speeches were given and the days were counted, and where the last kings, taken by Pedro de Alvarado, were questioned and put to death.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 4 (Brasseur 1861; Christenson 2003); not verbatim.

region.zh: 危地馬拉基切省庫馬爾卡赫（烏塔特蘭）

texts.period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03 (Quicab reigned c. 1425-75)

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 4, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

summary.en: Quicab, son of the lineage houses, is the great warrior-king of the K'iche': he burns the towns of the lowlands and the mountains, takes tribute and captives, and his wars are remembered as the measuring of the kingdom's borders — the sword that drew the map the Spanish inherited.
summary.zh: 奎卡布，族系之家的兒子，是基切的偉大戰爭之王：他焚燒低地與山地諸鎮，收取貢賦與俘虜；其戰事被記憶為王國邊界的測量——為西班牙人所繼承版圖的劃界之劍。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Quicab is the son of the lords of the council and the greatest of the K'iche' kings. He goes out from Rotten Cane with the warriors of the three lineages and burns the towns of the south coast and the mountains, and wherever his fires have passed, tribute is carried back to the rock city.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 4 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: His wars are counted like days: the towns taken are named one by one in the recitation, and the captives given to Tohil are named with them. Quicab rules long, and under him the borders of the K'iche' reach their widest measure, from the sea to the mountain passes of the north.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 4 (Brasseur 1861; Christenson 2003); not verbatim.
